questions.q: Which set lists only the changes that your book describes in a plant as it grows?
o: New leaves and branches emerge, its height increases and its stem thickens
New leaves emerge, its height increases and its stem becomes thinner
New leaves and branches emerge, its height increases and its roots become thinner
New branches emerge, its leaves become smaller and its stem thickens
questions.a: New leaves and branches emerge, its height increases and its stem thickens.

questions.q: In Activity 10.1, which pot usually has the plant with the maximum growth after two weeks?
o: Pot A, kept in direct sunlight and watered every day
Pot B, kept in direct sunlight without water
Pot C, kept in the dark and watered every day
All three pots, since the saplings were of similar size
questions.a: Pot A, kept in direct sunlight with adequate water, grows best because it gets both sunlight and water.

questions.q: In Activity 10.1, pot A is in direct sunlight with water, pot B is in direct sunlight without water, and pot C is in the dark with water. Consider the following statements. I. Pots B and C differ from each other only in water. II. Pots A and C differ from each other only in sunlight. III. Pot A, which gets both sunlight and water, is the pot that each of the other two pots is compared with. Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: II and III only. Statement I is wrong: pot B gets sunlight but no water while pot C gets water but no sunlight, so they differ in both conditions. Pot A gets both, so B is compared with A to see the role of water and C with A to see the role of sunlight.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The sapling in pot C grows as well as the sapling in pot A, because both are watered every day. Reason (R): Plants need both sunlight and water for their growth. Choose the correct option.
o: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
questions.a: A is false, but R is true. Pot C gets water but no sunlight, so its sapling grows less than the one in pot A; plants need both sunlight and water.

questions.q: True or False: In Activity 10.1, the leaves on each sapling are counted only once, after the two weeks are over. Give the verdict and a reason.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: the leaves are counted and recorded at the start (Day 1) and again after two weeks, so the change in each sapling can be seen
questions.a: False. The number of leaves on each sapling is counted and recorded at the start (Day 1) and again after two weeks (Table 10.1), so that the change in each sapling can be compared.

questions.q: (a) Name the two things that Activity 10.1 shows a plant needs for its growth. (b) Name any two features of the plants that are recorded in Table 10.1.
s: (a) Sunlight and water
(b) Any two of: height of the plant, number of leaves, colour of leaves
questions.a: (a) Sunlight and water. (b) Any two of: the height of the plant, the number of leaves and the colour of the leaves (green or yellow).

questions.q: Answer briefly about the set-up of Activity 10.1. (a) What kind of saplings does the book suggest planting in the pots? (b) Where is pot B kept, and is it watered? (c) For how long are the plants observed?
s: (a) Saplings of similar size of a fast-growing plant such as chilli or tomato
(b) Pot B is kept in direct sunlight and is not watered
(c) Two weeks
questions.a: (a) Saplings of similar size of a fast-growing plant such as chilli or tomato. (b) Pot B is kept in direct sunlight without adding water. (c) The plants are observed for two weeks.

questions.q: Three pots X, Y and Z were set up exactly like pots A, B and C of Activity 10.1, but the labels came off. All three saplings were 10 cm tall on Day 1. After two weeks: the sapling in X is 22 cm tall, the sapling in Y is 13 cm tall, and the sapling in Z has dried up and died. (a) Which pot was kept like pot A? Show the growth in cm. (b) Which pot was kept like pot C? Give a reason. (c) Which pot was kept like pot B? Give a reason.
s: (a) X: it grew 22 - 10 = 12 cm, the most, as pot A gets both sunlight and water
(b) Y: it grew only 13 - 10 = 3 cm, as pot C gets water but no sunlight and grows less
(c) Z: pot B gets sunlight but no water, and such a plant may die
questions.a: (a) X grew 12 cm (10 cm to 22 cm), the most, so it got both sunlight and water like pot A. (b) Y grew only 3 cm, so it got water but no sunlight, like pot C. (c) Z died, as a plant given sunlight but no water (pot B) may die.

questions.q: Meenal's class in Nagpur set up Activity 10.1 with three chilli saplings, each 8 cm tall with 5 leaves on Day 1. Pot A stood in direct sunlight and was watered daily. Pot B stood in direct sunlight with no water. Pot C was kept in a dark store room and watered daily. After two weeks the class recorded: pot A, 19 cm tall with 12 leaves; pot B, the sapling had dried up; pot C, 11 cm tall with 6 leaves. (a) Which pot's sapling grew the most, and by how many cm? (b) Which condition was missing for the sapling in pot B? (c) What conclusion does the class reach about plant growth? (d) Why were saplings of similar size used in all three pots?
s: (a) Pot A, which grew 19 - 8 = 11 cm
(b) Water was missing for pot B
(c) Plants need both sunlight and water for their growth
(d) So that any difference in growth comes from the different conditions, not from the saplings themselves
questions.a: (a) Pot A grew the most: from 8 cm to 19 cm, that is 11 cm. (b) Pot B got sunlight but no water. (c) Plants need both sunlight and water to grow. (d) Similar saplings make the comparison fair, so a difference in growth can be put down to the conditions alone.

questions.q: Rakesh tries Activity 10.1 as follows. Pot A: a tomato sapling 10 cm tall in direct sunlight, watered daily. Pot B: a chilli sapling 10 cm tall in direct sunlight, not watered. Pot C: a tomato sapling 20 cm tall in a dark room, watered only on alternate days. He concludes from his results that sunlight matters more than water. (a) What is wrong with the sapling chosen for pot B? (b) What is wrong with the sapling chosen for pot C? (c) What is wrong with the watering of pot C? (d) After fixing these, which pair of pots shows the role of water and which pair shows the role of sunlight? (e) Is his conclusion supported? What does the book's version of the activity show?
s: (a) Pot B has a different kind of plant (chilli); all pots should have the same kind of plant
(b) Pot C's sapling is twice as tall; saplings should be of similar size
(c) Pot C should be watered every day like pot A, so that only sunlight differs between A and C
(d) A and B show the role of water; A and C show the role of sunlight
(e) Not supported, as more than one thing was changed at a time; the activity shows plants need both sunlight and water
questions.a: (a) Pot B uses a chilli sapling while the others are tomato; all should be the same kind of plant. (b) Pot C's sapling is 20 cm, twice the others; saplings should be of similar size. (c) Pot C should be watered daily like pot A, so that the only difference between A and C is sunlight. (d) After the fixes, A and B differ only in water and A and C differ only in sunlight. (e) His conclusion is not supported, because each pot differed from A in more than one way; the proper activity shows that plants need both sunlight and water, not that one matters more.

questions.q: The green pigment in leaves that helps in capturing sunlight efficiently is called:
questions.a: Chlorophyll, the green pigment that makes leaves green and helps capture sunlight.

questions.q: Bhaskar wants to find out, using only leaves from his plant kept in sunlight, whether chlorophyll is needed to make starch. Which leaf should he test with iodine?
o: A leaf with both green and non-green patches
A leaf that is green all over
A green leaf from a plant kept in the dark for 36 hours
A leaf that is green all over, tested without decolourising it
questions.a: A leaf with both green and non-green patches: its two kinds of patches got the same sunlight and differ in chlorophyll, so comparing them shows whether chlorophyll is needed.

questions.q: Match each step of the starch test in Activity 10.2 (Column I) with its purpose (Column II). Column I: 1. Keeping the leaf in boiling water for five minutes 2. Placing the leaf in alcohol until it becomes colourless 3. Putting a few drops of diluted iodine solution on the leaf 4. Placing the alcohol test tube in a beaker of boiling water. Column II: A. Softens the leaf B. Removes the green colour so that a colour change is easy to see C. Shows starch by a blue-black colour D. Keeps the flammable alcohol away from direct heat
questions.a: 1-A, 2-B, 3-C, 4-D: boiling softens the leaf, alcohol decolourises it, iodine shows starch by a blue-black colour, and the water bath keeps flammable alcohol away from direct heat.

questions.q: Assertion (A): In Activity 10.2, the leaf is first kept in boiling water for five minutes. Reason (R): Alcohol is highly flammable and should never be placed near a heat source directly. Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A: the leaf is boiled to soften it; the flammability of alcohol explains why the alcohol test tube is heated in a beaker of boiling water.

questions.q: (a) In what form do plants store food? (b) Why are leaves called the 'food factories' of plants?
s: (a) As starch, a type of carbohydrate
(b) Starch is produced in the leaves, where chlorophyll helps prepare it in sunlight
questions.a: (a) Plants store food as starch, a type of carbohydrate. (b) Leaves are called food factories because starch is prepared in them, where chlorophyll helps make it in the presence of sunlight.

questions.q: In Activity 10.3 the green patches of the leaf from the plant kept in the dark for 36 hours did not turn blue-black. Juhi says: 'This happened because that leaf had no chlorophyll.' (a) Is Juhi right? Give a reason. (b) What was missing for that leaf, and what did this stop?
s: (a) No: the patches were green, so chlorophyll was present
(b) Sunlight was missing, so no starch was produced
questions.a: (a) Juhi is wrong: the patches were green, and leaves are green because of chlorophyll, so chlorophyll was present. (b) Sunlight was missing, because the plant was kept in the dark, so the leaf could not produce starch.

questions.q: Answer briefly. (a) What shape are leaves generally, by design? (b) In the iodine test, what does a blue-black colour on a decolourised leaf show? (c) Why do some leaves look red, violet or brown instead of green?
s: (a) Broad and flat
(b) The presence of starch
(c) They contain more of these coloured pigments than chlorophyll, which hides the green colour
questions.a: (a) Leaves are generally broad and flat. (b) A blue-black colour shows that starch is present. (c) Such leaves contain more red, violet or brown pigments than green chlorophyll, and these hide the green colour.

questions.q: In Activity 10.3, Bhaskar tested leaves with green and non-green patches, one from a plant kept in sunlight and one from a plant kept in the dark for 36 hours. (a) Which two patches should he compare to show that sunlight is needed for starch to form? (b) Which two patches should he compare to show that chlorophyll is needed? (c) Why does the non-green patch of the leaf from the dark tell him nothing new on its own?
s: (a) The green patch of the sunlit leaf (blue-black) and the green patch of the leaf from the dark (no change): only light differs
(b) The green and non-green patches of the sunlit leaf: only chlorophyll differs
(c) It lacks both sunlight and (enough) chlorophyll, so its result cannot be linked to either one
questions.a: (a) The green patch from the sunlit plant turned blue-black but the green patch from the dark plant did not; they differ only in light. (b) On the sunlit leaf, the green patch turned blue-black and the non-green patch did not; they differ only in chlorophyll. (c) The non-green patch from the dark lacked both light and enough chlorophyll, so its lack of starch cannot be blamed on either one.

questions.q: Kiran writes this report: 'I took a leaf with green and white patches from a plant that had been in a closed cupboard for two days. I did not note where its patches were. I softened it in boiling water and put it in alcohol, but I took it out while it was still green and put iodine on it. I could not see any blue-black colour, so leaves do not make starch.' Judge the report. (a) Why should he have recorded where the green and white patches were before the test? (b) What is wrong with testing the leaf while it is still green? (c) Even with a correct method, what result would you expect from this leaf, and why? (d) Is his final conclusion justified?
s: (a) After decolourising, the whole leaf looks colourless, so without a sketch (e.g. on tracing paper) he cannot tell which parts were green when he reads the result
(b) The green colour hides the colour change; the leaf should stay in alcohol until colourless
(c) No blue-black colour, because a plant kept in the dark does not produce starch
(d) Not justified: a leaf from a sunlit plant would turn blue-black on its green parts, showing leaves do make starch
questions.a: (a) Once decolourised the whole leaf is colourless, so he must sketch the green and white patches first (as Bhaskar did on tracing paper) to tell which parts were green. (b) A green leaf hides the colour change, so it must stay in alcohol until colourless. (c) Even if tested correctly, this leaf would not turn blue-black, because the plant was kept in the dark and could not make starch. (d) His conclusion is not justified; a properly tested leaf from a plant in sunlight turns blue-black on its green patches, showing that leaves make starch in sunlight.

questions.q: Riya tests a leaf with green and white patches, taken from a plant that stood in sunlight all day, for starch. Answer: (a) Why does she first keep the leaf in boiling water for five minutes? (b) In which liquid is the leaf then placed, and for how long? (c) After taking the leaf out, where does she place it, and what does she put on it? (d) After this, which patches turn blue-black? (e) What does this tell her about chlorophyll?
s: (a) To soften the leaf
(b) In alcohol, until the leaf becomes colourless
(c) On a plate; a few drops of diluted iodine solution, using a dropper
(d) Only the green patches turn blue-black
(e) Chlorophyll is needed to prepare starch in sunlight
questions.a: (a) Boiling softens the leaf. (b) The leaf is placed in alcohol until it becomes colourless. (c) She places the leaf on a plate and puts a few drops of diluted iodine solution on it with a dropper. (d) The green patches turn blue-black; the white patches do not. (e) Starch is made only where chlorophyll is present, so chlorophyll is needed to make starch in sunlight.

questions.q: The process by which plants prepare food in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll is called:
questions.a: Photosynthesis is the process by which plants prepare food in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll.

questions.q: Based on Activities 10.1 to 10.4, which set lists all the things found essential for the synthesis of food in plants?
o: Sunlight, water, chlorophyll and carbon dioxide
Sunlight, soil, chlorophyll and carbon dioxide
questions.a: Sunlight, water, chlorophyll and carbon dioxide are essential for the synthesis of food in plants.

questions.q: Read these statements about the set-up of Activity 10.4. I. The two halves of the leaf differ only in whether they get carbon dioxide. II. The plant is first kept in the dark for two to three days so that its leaves lose their chlorophyll. III. Because the plant was destarched first, any starch found in the leaf was made during the hours in sunlight. Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only. Statement II is wrong: the plant is kept in the dark so that it loses its stored starch (destarches), not its chlorophyll; the leaf must keep its chlorophyll to make starch.

questions.q: Assertion (A): In Activity 10.4, the half of the leaf inside the bottle does not turn blue-black with iodine. Reason (R): The half of the leaf inside the bottle gets no sunlight. Choose the correct option.
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: A is true, but R is false. The whole set-up is placed in sunlight; the inside half makes no starch because the caustic soda absorbs the carbon dioxide.

questions.q: True or False: Green parts of a plant other than the leaves can also carry out photosynthesis. Give the verdict and a reason.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the leaf is the primary site, but any other part that has chlorophyll also performs photosynthesis
questions.a: True. The leaf is the primary site of photosynthesis, but other parts of the plant that have chlorophyll also perform photosynthesis.

questions.q: In Activity 10.5, Barkha didi places her thumb on the mouth of the test tube while taking it off the set-up, and then quickly puts a lit matchstick into it. (a) Why does she cover the mouth with her thumb? (b) What does the intense flame of the matchstick tell her about the gas?
s: (a) So that the collected gas does not escape before it is tested
(b) The gas is rich in oxygen, so oxygen is released during photosynthesis
questions.a: (a) Covering the mouth keeps the collected gas from escaping before the test. (b) A matchstick burns with an intense flame in a gas rich in oxygen, so the gas released by the plant is oxygen.

questions.q: Answer briefly about Activity 10.4. (a) For how long is the potted plant kept in the dark first, and what does this do? (b) Which chemical is poured into the bottle, and what does it do? (c) Which half of the leaf turns blue-black with iodine?
s: (a) Two to three days, so that the plant destarches (loses its stored starch)
(b) Caustic soda (sodium hydroxide), which absorbs carbon dioxide from the air
(c) The half outside the bottle
questions.a: (a) Two to three days in the dark, so that the plant loses its stored starch. (b) Caustic soda (sodium hydroxide), which absorbs carbon dioxide. (c) The half of the leaf outside the bottle turns blue-black.

questions.q: Sohan sets up Activity 10.4 correctly with a destarched plant and caustic soda in the bottle, but he leaves the whole set-up in a dark room instead of in sunlight. After a few hours he tests the leaf with iodine. (a) Predict the colour of each half of the leaf. (b) Explain your prediction. (c) Can he conclude that carbon dioxide is essential for making starch? Give a reason.
s: (a) Neither half turns blue-black
(b) Without sunlight no starch is made in either half, and the plant had already lost its stored starch
(c) No: the outside half, which had carbon dioxide, also made no starch, so the two halves cannot show the effect of carbon dioxide
questions.a: (a) Neither half turns blue-black. (b) Sunlight is essential for making starch, so in the dark neither half makes any, and the destarched plant has no stored starch left. (c) No. The outside half had carbon dioxide but still made no starch, so the comparison between the halves no longer shows that carbon dioxide is needed.

questions.q: A teacher in Madurai sets up three beakers like Fig. 10.4, each with a funnel and an inverted test tube full of water. Set-up X has a water plant and stands in sunlight. Set-up Y has a similar water plant and stands in a dark cupboard. Set-up Z stands in sunlight next to X, but holds a plastic model of the water plant instead of a living one. After three hours, X has 4 cm of gas in its test tube, while Y and Z have no gas. (a) In which set-up was photosynthesis going on? (b) What would you see in the inverted test tube of X while the gas was being produced? (c) Mohan says the gas in X is only air that escaped from the water as the sun warmed it. Which set-up shows he is wrong, and how? (d) How can the teacher test that the gas in X is rich in oxygen, and what result is expected?
s: (a) X, the living plant in sunlight
(b) Air bubbles emerging from the plant and collecting in the inverted test tube
(c) Z: it was in the same sunlight but gave no gas, so the gas in X came from the living plant
(d) Insert a lit matchstick into the gas; it burns with an intense flame
questions.a: (a) X, where a living water plant got sunlight. (b) Air bubbles rise from the plant and collect at the top of the inverted test tube. (c) Z stood in the same sunlight and was warmed the same way but gave no gas; so the gas in X was made by the living plant, not air driven out of warm water. (d) Insert a lit matchstick into the collected gas; it burns with an intense flame, showing the gas is rich in oxygen.

questions.q: After Activities 10.4 and 10.5, three students write conclusions. Ravi: 'A leaf makes starch from carbon dioxide alone.' Seema: 'A water plant gives out oxygen whether it is in sunlight or in the dark.' Tara: 'Activity 10.4 shows carbon dioxide is essential for starch, and Activity 10.5 shows oxygen is released in photosynthesis, which needs sunlight.' (a) Judge Ravi's conclusion, naming the other things the leaf needed. (b) Judge Seema's conclusion using the two set-ups of Activity 10.5. (c) Judge Tara's conclusion. (d) In Activity 10.4, what did the half of the leaf inside the bottle still have, and why does this matter? (e) Which result from Activity 10.3 gives further support to Tara's point that sunlight is needed?
s: (a) Ravi is wrong: water, sunlight and chlorophyll are also essential
(b) Seema is wrong: bubbles came only from set-up A in sunlight; set-up B in the dark gave none
(c) Tara is right on both points
(d) Water, sunlight and chlorophyll; only carbon dioxide was missing, so the lack of starch is due to carbon dioxide
(e) The green patches of the leaf from the plant kept in the dark for 36 hours did not turn blue-black with iodine
questions.a: (a) Ravi is wrong: carbon dioxide is essential but so are water, sunlight and chlorophyll. (b) Seema is wrong: bubbles of oxygen collected only in set-up A in sunlight, not in set-up B in the dark. (c) Tara is right. (d) The inside half still had water, sunlight and chlorophyll; only carbon dioxide was removed, so its lack of starch shows carbon dioxide is needed. (e) In Activity 10.3 the green patches of the leaf from the plant kept in the dark for 36 hours did not turn blue-black, so no starch was made without sunlight.

questions.q: During photosynthesis, food is actually produced in the form of:
questions.a: Glucose, a simple carbohydrate; it is later converted into starch for storage.

questions.q: A money plant grows in a glass jar of water on a sunny window, with no soil at all, and stays green and healthy. Which statement best explains how it gets what it needs for photosynthesis?
o: Its roots take in water from the jar, its leaves take in carbon dioxide from the air, and the window gives it sunlight
It takes ready-made food from the water in the jar through its roots
It does not need water for photosynthesis, only sunlight and air
It takes in carbon dioxide through its roots from the water in the jar
questions.a: Its roots take in water from the jar, its leaves take in carbon dioxide from the air through the stomata, and sunlight comes through the window, so it can photosynthesise without soil.

questions.q: Consider the following statements. I. Photosynthesis produces glucose and oxygen. II. Stomata are tiny pores on the surface of leaves. III. Glucose is a simple carbohydrate that later gets converted into starch for storage. Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I, II and III. Photosynthesis produces glucose and oxygen, stomata are tiny pores on leaf surfaces, and glucose is a simple carbohydrate that is later converted into starch for storage.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A leaf exchanges gases through its stomata even when it is not photosynthesising. Reason (R): Stomata help in the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide during both photosynthesis and respiration. Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: a leaf respires even when it is not photosynthesising, and the stomata help exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide in respiration too.

questions.q: Match each item in Column I with what the chapter tells about it in Column II. Column I: 1. Rustom Hormusji Dastur 2. Stomata 3. Glucose 4. Royal Institute of Science, Bombay. Column II: A. Studied the effects of water, temperature and the colour of light on photosynthesis B. Tiny pores on the surface of leaves that help in the exchange of gases C. A simple carbohydrate produced in photosynthesis D. Now called the Institute of Science, Mumbai
questions.a: 1-A, 2-B, 3-C, 4-D: Dastur studied water, temperature and the colour of light in photosynthesis; stomata are tiny pores for gas exchange; glucose is the simple carbohydrate made in photosynthesis; the Royal Institute of Science, Bombay is now the Institute of Science, Mumbai.

questions.q: Write the word equation of photosynthesis. Show what is written above and below the arrow.
s: Carbon dioxide + Water gives Glucose + Oxygen
Sunlight and chlorophyll shown on the arrow as the conditions
questions.a: Carbon dioxide + Water -> Glucose + Oxygen, with sunlight written above the arrow and chlorophyll below it.

questions.q: True or False: The water a leaf uses in photosynthesis enters the leaf through its stomata, along with carbon dioxide. Give the verdict and a reason.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: water (with minerals) is taken up from the soil by the roots; stomata help in the exchange of gases
questions.a: False. Water, along with minerals, is taken up from the soil by the roots; the stomata are for the exchange of gases such as carbon dioxide and oxygen.

questions.q: Two leaves are picked from the same well-watered potted plant: leaf L1 at 6 am after a long night, and leaf L2 at 5 pm after a sunny day. Both are tested with iodine, and L2 shows a much deeper blue-black colour than L1. (a) In what form is food first made in a leaf, and what is it later converted into? (b) Explain why L2 had more starch. (c) In Activity 10.4 a plant is kept in the dark for two to three days to destarch it. Use this to explain why L1 had less starch.
s: (a) As glucose, a simple carbohydrate; it is later converted into starch for storage
(b) Through the sunny day the leaf carried out photosynthesis, making glucose that was converted into starch and stored
(c) In the dark there is no photosynthesis, so no new starch is made, and a plant in the dark loses its stored starch; after the night less was left in L1
questions.a: (a) Food is first made as glucose, which is later converted into starch for storage. (b) During the sunny day L2's leaf photosynthesised, and the glucose it made was stored as starch. (c) A plant in the dark makes no new food and loses its stored starch, which is why a plant is destarched by keeping it in the dark; so after a whole night L1 had less starch left.

questions.q: In her school lab, Neha follows Activity 10.6 to look at a leaf peel under a microscope. Answer: (a) From which surface of the leaf is the thin peel taken? (b) What is put on the peel to make it easier to see? (c) What are the tiny pores she sees called? (d) Name the two gases these pores help to exchange.
s: (a) The lower surface of the leaf
(b) A drop of ink
(c) Stomata
(d) Oxygen and carbon dioxide
questions.a: (a) The peel is taken from the lower surface of the leaf. (b) A drop of ink is put on it. (c) The tiny pores are stomata. (d) They help exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide.

questions.q: A farmer near Belagavi grows beetroot, whose swollen root stores food, in two plots with the same soil, the same seeds and the same daily watering. Plot P is in open sunlight. Plot Q is covered by a shade net that lets in much less sunlight. At harvest the average beetroot from plot P weighs 240 g and the average beetroot from plot Q weighs 96 g. (a) In which part of the plant is the food stored in a beetroot made, and as what substance? (b) Through which tubes does this food reach the root, and in what form is it stored there? (c) How many times heavier is the average beetroot from plot P than from plot Q? (d) Explain this difference. (e) A neighbour says: 'The food in a beetroot comes from the soil through its roots.' Use the two plots to decide whether he is right.
s: (a) In the leaves, as glucose made by photosynthesis
(b) Through the phloem; it is stored as starch
(d) Only sunlight differed; with less sunlight the leaves in plot Q made less food by photosynthesis, so less reached the root
(e) He is wrong: the soil and water were the same, yet the roots differed with sunlight, so the stored food was made in the leaves using sunlight
questions.a: (a) The food is made in the leaves by photosynthesis, as glucose. (b) It is carried from the leaves through the phloem and stored in the root as starch. (c) 240 / 96 = 2.5, so plot P's average beetroot is 2.5 times heavier. (d) The two plots differed only in sunlight; photosynthesis needs sunlight, so the shaded leaves made less food and less was sent to the roots. (e) The neighbour is wrong: both plots had the same soil and water, yet the beetroots differed when only sunlight differed, so the stored food was made in the leaves using sunlight, not taken from the soil.

questions.q: The thin tube-like structures that carry water and minerals from the roots to the other parts of a plant are called:
questions.a: Xylem carries water and minerals from the roots to other parts of the plant.

questions.q: In Activity 10.7, a red colour appears in the stem, leaves and flowers of the twig kept in red ink water. What does this show?
o: Water moves up the stem and reaches the leaves and flowers
Food made in the leaves moves down into the water
The flowers make the red colour themselves
The twig in plain water takes in no water at all
questions.a: The red ink travelled with the water up the stem to the leaves and flowers, showing that water moves up through the plant.

questions.q: Match each event in a carrot plant (Column I) with the part that does the job (Column II). Column I: 1. A mineral from fertiliser in the soil travels up to the leaves 2. Food made in the leaves reaches the carrot to be stored 3. Carbon dioxide from the air enters a leaf 4. Water in the soil is first taken into the plant. Column II: A. Xylem B. Phloem C. Stomata D. Roots
questions.a: 1-A, 2-B, 3-C, 4-D: minerals dissolved in water rise in the xylem, food goes to the carrot through the phloem, carbon dioxide enters through the stomata, and water is taken up by the roots.

questions.q: (a) Name the tubes that carry the food made in the leaves to all parts of a plant. (b) Name two parts of a plant where the transported food may be stored.
s: (a) Phloem
(b) Seeds and roots
questions.a: (a) The phloem carries food from the leaves to all parts of the plant. (b) Food may be stored in parts such as seeds and roots.

questions.q: (a) Which part of a plant takes up water and minerals from the soil? (b) Why are minerals needed by plants?
s: (a) The roots
(b) Minerals are important nutrients for the growth of plants
questions.a: (a) The roots take up water along with minerals from the soil. (b) Minerals are important nutrients needed for plant growth.

questions.q: Answer briefly about Activity 10.7. (a) What kind of twigs does the book suggest using? (b) What is added to tumbler B? (c) How and where are the stems cut before placing them in the tumblers?
s: (a) Twigs of two similar tender plants, preferably with white flowers, such as white sadabahar or balsam
(b) A few drops of red ink
(c) Cut obliquely at the base while the stems are kept inside the water
questions.a: (a) Twigs of two similar tender plants, preferably with white flowers, such as white sadabahar or balsam. (b) A few drops of red ink are added to tumbler B. (c) The stems are cut obliquely at their base while kept inside the water, and placed in the tumblers at once.

questions.q: Compare the xylem and the phloem of a plant on three points: (a) what each carries, (b) from where each mainly carries it, and (c) which activity or observation in the chapter gives evidence for the xylem's job.
s: (a) Xylem carries water and dissolved minerals; phloem carries food
(b) Xylem carries them from the roots upward; phloem carries food from the leaves to all parts
(c) Activity 10.7: red ink water rose up the twig and red was seen in the cut stem's xylem
questions.a: (a) Xylem carries water and minerals; phloem carries food. (b) Xylem carries water and minerals from the roots to the stem, branches and leaves; phloem carries food from the leaves to all parts, including storage parts like seeds and roots. (c) In Activity 10.7 the red ink water rose up the stem, and red colour was seen in the thin tubes (xylem) of the cut stem.

questions.q: The science club of a school in Pune repeats Activity 10.7 with two similar white sadabahar twigs, but uses blue ink in place of red ink. Tumbler A has plain water and tumbler B has water with a few drops of blue ink. The next day the petals of the twig in tumbler B show blue streaks, while the twig in tumbler A looks unchanged. When the stem of the B twig is cut above the water level, blue dots are seen in it under a magnifying glass. (a) Name the tubes that carried the coloured water up the stem. (b) Why was the twig in tumbler A kept? (c) Name one other thing that travels up the stem in the same tubes. (d) Besides the petals, in which other parts of the B twig would you expect to see the blue colour, and why?
s: (a) The xylem
(b) For comparison: it shows that the blue colour comes from the ink and not from the twig itself
(c) Minerals dissolved in water
(d) In the stem and the leaves, because the xylem is present in the stem, branches and leaves
questions.a: (a) The xylem carried the coloured water up. (b) Twig A is the comparison: it got plain water and stayed unchanged, so the blue colour in B came from the ink. (c) Minerals dissolved in water travel up the xylem in the same way. (d) In the stem and the leaves as well, because the xylem runs through the stem, branches and leaves of the plant.

questions.q: A farmer wants his chilli plants to get more minerals. His neighbour advises: 'Sprinkle the dry fertiliser on the leaves, because the leaves are where the plant makes its food. And do not water the field afterwards, or the water will wash the fertiliser away.' Judge this advice. (a) Which part of the plant takes up minerals, and from where? (b) In what form do minerals travel inside the plant, and through which tubes? (c) Is the advice not to water sensible? Explain. (d) Give your advice to the farmer.
s: (a) The roots take up minerals, dissolved in water, from the soil
(b) Minerals travel dissolved in water, up through the xylem to the stem, branches and leaves
(c) No: minerals move with water, so watering helps them dissolve and be taken up and carried by the xylem
(d) Put the fertiliser in the soil near the roots and water it
questions.a: (a) Minerals are taken up from the soil by the roots, dissolved in water. (b) They travel dissolved in water through the xylem to the stem, branches and leaves. (c) Not sensible: minerals move along with water, so water is needed for the roots to take them up and for the xylem to carry them. (d) The farmer should put the fertiliser in the soil near the roots and water the field.

questions.q: A pea plant grows in a farm in Ooty. Describe the journey of water and food in it by answering: (a) Which part takes up water and minerals from the soil? (b) Through which tubes do they travel upward? (c) Name two places in the plant where these tubes are present. (d) Through which tubes does food made in the leaves travel? (e) In which part of the pea plant, that we eat, is much of its food stored?
s: (a) The roots
(b) The xylem
(c) Any two of: stem, branches, leaves
(d) The phloem
(e) In its seeds, the peas
questions.a: (a) The roots take up water and minerals. (b) They travel up through the xylem. (c) The xylem is present in the stem, branches and leaves. (d) Food made in the leaves travels through the phloem. (e) The pea plant stores much of its food in its seeds, the peas we eat.

questions.q: Lime water turns milky when it gets more of which gas?
questions.a: Carbon dioxide; in Activity 10.8 the lime water turns milky because of the extra carbon dioxide from the respiring seeds.

questions.q: Two word equations are written with two substances hidden. Photosynthesis: P + Water gives Q + Oxygen (in sunlight, with chlorophyll). Respiration: Q + Oxygen gives P + Water + Energy. What are P and Q?
o: P is carbon dioxide and Q is glucose
P is glucose and Q is carbon dioxide
P is oxygen and Q is starch
P is starch and Q is carbon dioxide
questions.a: P is carbon dioxide and Q is glucose: photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and water to make glucose and oxygen, and respiration breaks down glucose with oxygen to give carbon dioxide, water and energy.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The roots of a plant need oxygen even though they are not green. Reason (R): All parts of a plant, green or non-green, carry out respiration, in which glucose is broken down using oxygen. Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: roots respire like every other part, and respiration uses oxygen.

questions.q: Consider the following statements about respiration in plants. I. A root, which is not green, still breaks down glucose using oxygen. II. Soaked moong seeds kept in the dark for 24 hours give out no carbon dioxide, because they cannot photosynthesise there. III. Respiration gives out oxygen, and this is why the lime water in Activity 10.8 turns milky. Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I only. II is wrong: the seeds respire in the dark and release carbon dioxide, which is why the lime water turns milky. III is wrong: respiration uses oxygen and releases carbon dioxide; carbon dioxide turns lime water milky.

questions.q: (a) Which substance is broken down in respiration, and with the help of which gas? (b) What do plants use the energy released in respiration for?
s: (a) Glucose, broken down in the presence of oxygen
(b) For their growth and development
questions.a: (a) Glucose is broken down in the presence of oxygen. (b) Plants use the energy for their growth and development.

questions.q: Sprouting potatoes are kept in a dark store room, and their white sprouts grow longer day by day. (a) Name the process that releases the energy for this growth, and the food substance broken down in it. (b) Name the gas the potato uses in this process and the gas it gives out.
s: (a) Respiration; glucose (from the food stored in the potato) is broken down
(b) It uses oxygen and gives out carbon dioxide
questions.a: (a) Respiration releases the energy for growth; in it glucose, from the food stored in the potato, is broken down. (b) The potato uses oxygen and gives out carbon dioxide (with water) in respiration.

questions.q: Answer briefly. (a) Write the word equation of respiration. (b) Name the gas that a plant uses in respiration. (c) Which parts of a plant carry out respiration?
s: (a) Glucose + Oxygen gives Carbon dioxide + Water + Energy
(b) Oxygen
(c) All parts, green or non-green
questions.a: (a) Glucose + Oxygen -> Carbon dioxide + Water + Energy. (b) Oxygen. (c) All parts of a plant, green or non-green, carry out respiration.

questions.q: Imran sets up three sealed glass jars of pond water, each with a carbon dioxide indicator whose colour chart gives a level from 1 (very little carbon dioxide) to 10 (a lot). Jar J1 holds a sprig of a water plant and stands on a sunny window sill. Jar J2 holds a similar sprig and stands in a dark cupboard. Jar J3 holds only pond water and stands next to J1. All three start at level 5. After 4 hours J1 is at level 2, J2 is at level 8 and J3 is still at level 5. (a) Why is jar J3 kept? (b) Which process explains the fall in J1? (c) Explain the rise in J2. (d) Imran says: 'The plant in J1 has stopped respiring, because its carbon dioxide fell.' Use the data to decide whether he is right.
s: (a) As the comparison: pond water alone stayed at 5, so the changes in J1 and J2 are caused by the plant
(b) Photosynthesis in sunlight takes in carbon dioxide
(c) In the dark there is no photosynthesis, but the plant still respires and releases carbon dioxide (5 to 8)

(d) Not right: all living parts respire all the time; J2 shows this plant gives out carbon dioxide, and in J1 photosynthesis used carbon dioxide faster than respiration released it, so the level fell by 3
questions.a: (a) J3, with pond water only, stayed at level 5, so the changes in J1 and J2 come from the plant. (b) In sunlight the water plant photosynthesises and takes in carbon dioxide, so J1 fell from 5 to 2. (c) In the dark the plant cannot photosynthesise but still respires, releasing carbon dioxide, so J2 rose from 5 to 8. (d) Imran is wrong: all living parts of a plant respire, and J2 shows this plant gives out carbon dioxide; in J1 photosynthesis used up carbon dioxide faster than respiration released it, so the level fell overall.

questions.q: A seed shop in Indore keeps two sacks of moong. Sack 1 holds dry seeds. Sack 2 got wet in the rain, and its seeds have started to germinate. The shopkeeper's daughter pumps air from inside each sack through lime water in two separate test tubes. The lime water from sack 2 turns milky within a few minutes, while the lime water from sack 1 hardly changes. (a) Which life process is going on actively in sack 2? (b) Why does the lime water from sack 2 turn milky? (c) What substance in the seeds is broken down to release energy in this process? (d) The shopkeeper wants to store wet seeds for two months to sell later. Should he dry them first? Justify your decision.
s: (a) Respiration by the germinating seeds
(b) Respiration releases carbon dioxide, and more carbon dioxide turns lime water milky
(c) Glucose (from the seeds' stored food), broken down using oxygen
(d) Yes: germinating seeds keep respiring and breaking down their food for growth, so drying them keeps the stored food from being used up
questions.a: (a) The germinating seeds in sack 2 are respiring actively. (b) Respiration gives out carbon dioxide; the extra carbon dioxide turns the lime water milky. (c) Glucose is broken down with oxygen to release energy. (d) He should dry them first: wet, germinating seeds go on respiring and using their food for growth, so seeds stored wet would lose the food they hold and start to sprout.

questions.q: Three classmates make claims about respiration in plants. Arun: 'Plants respire only at night, because in the day they photosynthesise instead.' Bela: 'Only the green leaves of a plant respire.' Charu: 'Respiration in plants gives out oxygen, just like photosynthesis.' (a) Judge Arun's claim. (b) Judge Bela's claim, using Activity 10.8 as evidence. (c) Judge Charu's claim. (d) Write the word equation of respiration that settles Charu's claim. (e) State in one sentence how photosynthesis and respiration differ in where they occur.
s: (a) Wrong: respiration does not stop when photosynthesis runs; all living parts respire to get energy for growth
(b) Wrong: all parts respire; non-green germinating moong seeds in the dark gave out carbon dioxide in Activity 10.8
(c) Wrong: respiration uses oxygen and gives out carbon dioxide
(d) Glucose + Oxygen gives Carbon dioxide + Water + Energy
(e) Photosynthesis occurs only in green parts in sunlight, while respiration occurs in all living parts
questions.a: (a) Arun is wrong: respiration does not stop when photosynthesis runs; all living parts of a plant respire to get energy for growth. (b) Bela is wrong: all parts, green or non-green, respire; the non-green moong seeds in the dark released carbon dioxide in Activity 10.8. (c) Charu is wrong: respiration uses oxygen and releases carbon dioxide. (d) Glucose + Oxygen -> Carbon dioxide + Water + Energy. (e) Photosynthesis takes place only in the green parts in sunlight, while respiration takes place in every living part of the plant.
